lessons.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Predict Phase: Where Do the Bubbles Come From?

quiz.prompt: Mwalimu Njoroge's class put one freshly cut sukuma wiki leaf in warm water (about 42°C) and a similar leaf in cold water (about 15°C). What did the class observe?
choices: More bubbles came from the leaf in the cold water than from the leaf in the warm water
More bubbles came from the leaf in the warm water than from the leaf in the cold water
Only the leaf in the cold water gave bubbles
Both leaves gave exactly the same number of bubbles
quiz.rationale: The phenomenon showed streams of bubbles in warm water and far fewer in cold water. This question only checks the observation, not the reason for it.
quiz.placement: Observe: groups submerge one leaf in warm water and one in cold water and compare bubbles

quiz.prompt: Students watched submerged sukuma wiki leaves and recorded where the bubbles appeared. Which statement matches what they observed?
choices: Bubbles streamed from particular points on the leaf, not evenly from the whole surface
Bubbles came only from the water around the leaf, never from the leaf
Bubbles came off evenly from the whole leaf surface at once
Bubbles appeared only after the leaf had been in the water for one hour
quiz.rationale: The anchoring phenomenon is that bubbles stream from specific points on the leaf surface. Students marked these spots on their leaf outline diagrams.
quiz.placement: Observe: students mark exactly where bubbles appear on the leaf outline diagram

quiz.prompt: During the observation, the teacher said, "Record exactly where bubbles appear, not why." Which note written by a student is an observation and not an explanation?
choices: "The warm water is boiling the leaf."
"Bubbles streamed from small spots on the leaf, and there were more streams in the warm beaker."
"The bubbles are oxygen."
"The leaf is breathing out like our lungs."
quiz.rationale: An observation records what can be seen or counted, such as where the bubbles appear and how many there are. The other notes are ideas about why, or what the gas is, and have not been tested yet.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured observation with annotated diagram (separating where from why)

quiz.prompt: A group wants a fair comparison of bubbles in warm and cold water. Which set-up is best?
choices: Two fresh sukuma wiki leaves of similar size, one in warm water and one in cold water, watched for the same 5 minutes
Two sukuma wiki leaves of similar size, both in warm water, watched for different lengths of time
One large sukuma wiki leaf in warm water and one small leaf in cold water
A sukuma wiki leaf in warm water and a different type of leaf in cold water
quiz.rationale: A fair comparison changes only the water temperature. The leaf type, leaf size and observation time stay the same.
quiz.placement: Observe: two beakers (warm ~42°C and cold ~15°C) with two leaves of similar size, observed for 5 minutes

quiz.prompt: After the observation, a student asks, "What gas is inside the bubbles?" At this point in the unit, which response is best?
choices: It is definitely carbon dioxide, so write that down.
It is definitely oxygen, so write that down.
It is only air stuck on the outside of the leaf, so the question does not matter.
We have not explained that yet. We will look for evidence in later lessons.
quiz.rationale: This is the anchoring lesson, so the gas is deliberately left unexplained. Students record the question and keep it for the unit investigation instead of being given an answer.
quiz.placement: Explain: introducing the unit driving question and saying today's observation is only the first clue

quiz.prompt: On the Driving Question Board, which blue "What I wonder" note is the most useful, investigable question about the sukuma wiki bubbles?
choices: Do all kinds of leaves produce the same number of bubbles in warm water?
Why is biology hard?
Who made the first beaker?
Is sukuma wiki tasty?
quiz.rationale: A productive wonder question can be investigated by testing leaves in warm and cold water. The other questions are not about the phenomenon or cannot be tested with the lesson's materials.
quiz.placement: DQB: students write 'What I noticed', 'What I wonder' and 'What I think I already know' sticky notes

quiz.prompt: Students draw an initial model of a sukuma wiki leaf and write at the bottom: "I am not sure about ___." Why do they write this?
choices: It shows what they still need to find out, so they can revise the model in later lessons
The teacher will give the full answer at the end of this lesson
The model will be marked wrong unless every part is correct
Parts they are unsure about must be rubbed out before the model is shown to a partner
quiz.rationale: The initial model is not graded. It is a baseline of honest thinking, and the 'not sure' statement points to what students will investigate and revise during the unit.
quiz.placement: Model: students draw their first Initial Model of a sukuma wiki leaf cross-section

lessons.title: Sites of Gaseous Exchange in Plants

quiz.prompt: Mwalimu Njoroge's class submerged fresh sukuma wiki leaves in warm water and saw bubbles streaming from specific spots on the leaf surface. Which structure are these spots?
choices: Stomata, small pores in the leaf epidermis
Pneumatophores, upward-growing roots
The waxy cuticle, which covers the whole leaf
Lenticels, raised spots on the leaf
quiz.rationale: Gas leaves a leaf through stomata, which are small pores mostly in the lower epidermis. Lenticels are on woody stems, pneumatophores are roots, and the cuticle is a continuous waxy layer that limits gas exchange.
quiz.placement: Predict: re-examining the anchor photograph of bubbles on sukuma wiki leaves and sorting predictions into 'Whole surface' vs 'Specific spots'

quiz.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a plant structure with where it is found?
choices: Pneumatophores: the stomatal pores of a leaf
Lenticels: the lower epidermis of a leaf
Stomata: the bark of woody stems
Lenticels: woody stems, such as the bark of a mango tree
quiz.rationale: Lenticels are small raised pores in the bark of woody stems. Stomata are in leaf epidermis, and pneumatophores are the breathing roots of mangroves.
quiz.placement: Observe Part A: READ-MARK-NOTE guided reading on sites of gaseous exchange

quiz.prompt: Mangrove trees at Mida Creek, Kilifi, grow roots that stick upward out of the muddy water. Why is this an advantage for the tree?
choices: The roots can take in air above the water line, because the mud has very little oxygen
The roots can stop water from entering the tree
The roots can store carbon dioxide for the leaves
The roots can make food by photosynthesis in the mud
quiz.rationale: Pneumatophores rise above the water and mud so that gases can enter and leave the roots. Waterlogged mud holds very little air.
quiz.placement: Observe Part B: animation paused at pneumatophores (mangroves at Mida Creek)

quiz.prompt: What do guard cells do in a leaf?
choices: They open and close the stomata to control gas movement
They store air in the spongy mesophyll
They make the waxy cuticle on the leaf surface
They carry water from the roots to the leaf
quiz.rationale: Guard cells surround each stomatal pore and change shape to open or close it, controlling gas exchange and water loss.
quiz.placement: Observe Part B: animation paused at stomata, watching the guard cells open and close

quiz.prompt: Learners labelling a leaf cross-section placed 'stomata' on the lower epidermis, with a guard cell on each side of the pore. Which description of the stomata is the best?
choices: Air spaces between the palisade cells
Solid cells that stop all gases entering the leaf
Openings controlled by guard cells that let CO₂ in and O₂ out
Waxy layers that stop water entering the leaf
quiz.rationale: Stomata are pores whose opening is controlled by guard cells. They allow gases to move in and out, so they are not just 'holes' and not a barrier.
quiz.placement: Explain: group labelling of the leaf cross-section with label cards and one-sentence functional descriptions

quiz.prompt: Why is the waxy cuticle an advantage for a sukuma wiki plant growing under the hot Nairobi sun?
choices: It reduces water loss from the leaf surface
It opens the stomata wider in hot weather
It lets more carbon dioxide pass through the leaf surface
It absorbs water from the air into the leaf
quiz.rationale: The cuticle is waxy and waterproof, so it limits water loss, which is vital in warm climates. It also limits gas exchange through the leaf surface, so gases mainly use the stomata.
quiz.placement: Explain: Connect-Back question 3 on the waxy cuticle

quiz.prompt: After today's lesson, a student claims: 'Plants only breathe through their roots.' Which statement best corrects this?
choices: Plants exchange gases only through the waxy cuticle
Plants exchange gases only through stomata on the stem
Plants do not exchange gases with their environment
Plants exchange gases through several sites: stomata in leaves, lenticels on woody stems and pneumatophores in some roots
quiz.rationale: Plants exchange gases through several structures: stomata (leaves), lenticels (woody stems) and pneumatophores (mangrove roots). Roots are not the only site.
quiz.placement: DQB: group 'We now know...' statements and checking for misconceptions

quiz.prompt: A group is building a leaf cross-section model. The pores they punched should be on the lower epidermis, each with a clay guard cell on either side. Where should they also show space for gases to move after entering through the pores?
choices: Air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
Inside the waxy cuticle
Outside the leaf, below the lower epidermis
Inside the guard cells only
quiz.rationale: After gases enter through stomata they move through the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll to reach the cells. A complete model must show these spaces.
quiz.placement: Model: building the 3D leaf cross-section model with cardboard, cellophane and clay

lessons.title: Stomatal Mechanisms: How Guard Cells Control Gas Exchange

quiz.prompt: Bubbles came from the stomata on sukuma wiki leaves. Which statement is the best scientific idea about what makes guard cells open a stomatal pore?
choices: Water moves into the guard cells, so they swell and become turgid and the pore opens
Gases pushing against the guard cells force the pore open
The plant decides to open the pore when it wants gas
The pore opens when guard cells lose water and become flaccid
quiz.rationale: Guard cells open the pore when water enters them by osmosis and they become turgid. Saying the plant 'decides' is a vague idea, not a mechanism.
quiz.placement: Predict: 3-sentence prediction journal on what triggers guard cell movement

quiz.prompt: In the potassium ion theory, K+ ions are actively pumped into guard cells in the light. What happens next?
choices: The water potential inside the guard cells falls, so water enters by osmosis and the guard cells become turgid
The water potential inside the guard cells stays the same, so the pore stays closed
The water potential inside the guard cells rises, so water leaves by osmosis and the guard cells become flaccid
The K+ ions move water in by active transport, with no osmosis involved
quiz.rationale: More solute (K+) inside lowers the water potential in the guard cells. Water then moves in by osmosis, the cells become turgid and the pore opens. Many students wrongly think a high solute concentration means high water potential.
quiz.placement: Observe: Animation 1 (potassium ion theory), pause-and-sketch of K+ and water movement

quiz.prompt: In the starch-sugar hypothesis, what happens to the guard cells in the light, and why does the pore open?
choices: Sugars are pumped out of the guard cells, so the pore opens because the cells are lighter
Starch stays unchanged, but K+ ions move out, so the guard cells become flaccid and the pore opens
Starch is changed into soluble sugars, which lowers the water potential, so water enters by osmosis and the guard cells become turgid
Soluble sugars are changed into starch, which raises the water potential, so water leaves and the pore opens
quiz.rationale: In the light, starch is converted to soluble sugars. This lowers the water potential in the guard cells, so water enters by osmosis and the guard cells become turgid. In darkness the sugars change back to starch.
quiz.placement: Observe: Animation 2 (starch-sugar hypothesis) and the two-column comparison table

quiz.prompt: Three ideas explain how guard cells open: the photosynthetic theory, the starch-sugar hypothesis and the potassium ion theory. Which step is the same in all three?
choices: Guard cells lose water in the light so that the pore opens
More solute builds up in the guard cells and water follows it in by osmosis
Water is pumped into guard cells directly using ATP
Guard cells use K+ ions as the only solute
quiz.rationale: In all three ideas the guard cells gain solutes (sugars from photosynthesis, sugars from starch, or K+ ions). This lowers the water potential, and water follows by osmosis. The theories differ in the source of the solutes.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher adds the photosynthetic theory after Animation 2 and asks which step is the same in all three ideas

quiz.prompt: A maize seedling in a shamba near Kisumu wilts at noon on a hot sunny day, and its stomata close. Which explanation fits the potassium ion theory?
choices: K+ ions move into the guard cells, so water enters and the guard cells become turgid and close the pore
K+ ions stay in the guard cells, but water is pumped out using sunlight energy
K+ ions move out of the guard cells, so water enters by osmosis and the pore closes
K+ ions move out of the guard cells, so water leaves by osmosis, the guard cells become flaccid and the pore closes
quiz.rationale: When K+ leaves the guard cells, their water potential rises and water moves out by osmosis. The guard cells lose turgor, become flaccid and the pore closes, which reduces water loss.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER scenario card on the maize seedling near Kisumu that wilts at noon and recovers at dusk

quiz.prompt: Students in Nairobi saw more bubbles from sukuma wiki leaves in warm water. Which chain of events correctly links guard cell action to the gas escaping as bubbles?
choices: Water leaves the guard cells, they become flaccid, the pore opens, and more gas escapes
K+ enters the guard cells, water enters by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid, the pore opens, and more gas escapes
The pore opens first, then K+ enters the guard cells, then water enters and more gas escapes
Gas escapes first, which makes the guard cells turgid, and then the pore opens
quiz.rationale: The mechanism runs in order: K+ moves in, water follows by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid, the pore opens, and more gas can leave the leaf. This is the kind of causal chain that links the mechanism to the bubbles.
quiz.placement: DQB: writing connection notes that link today's mechanism to the Lesson 1 bubble observation

quiz.prompt: A student draws a zoomed-in model of a stomatal pore that is OPEN. The guard cells are labelled turgid, but the K+ arrows point out of the guard cells. What is the error?
choices: The K+ arrows are correct, because K+ leaving draws water in
The arrows should show water moving out of the guard cells, because turgid cells lose water
The K+ arrows should point into the guard cells, because K+ entering lowers the water potential and water follows in
The guard cells should be labelled flaccid, because an open pore means the guard cells have lost water
quiz.rationale: An open pore needs turgid guard cells. This needs K+ to move in, which lowers the water potential so water moves in by osmosis. K+ arrows pointing out show the closed state.
quiz.placement: Model: error-detection task on the projected inset with K+ arrows pointing outward on an open pore

lessons.title: Aerobic & Anaerobic Respiration — Research, Experiment & Data Analysis

quiz.prompt: Two bags hold fresh sukuma wiki leaves. One bag is in light. The other is wrapped in black polythene, so no light reaches the leaves, but it still contains air. Photosynthesis cannot happen in the dark bag. Where does the carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the dark bag come from?
choices: There is no CO₂ in the dark bag because plants only make CO₂ in light
From respiration in the leaf cells, which goes on in light and in darkness
From photosynthesis, which carries on slowly in the dark
From the black polythene, which gives off CO₂
quiz.rationale: Respiration happens in living cells all the time and releases CO₂, so CO₂ is made in the dark even though photosynthesis stops. Photosynthesis uses CO₂ and needs light.
quiz.placement: Predict: two sealed bags of sukuma wiki (light bag and black polythene bag) and the Think-Pair-Share predictions

quiz.prompt: A mandazi vendor in Gikomba Market notices that her dough rises faster on a warm day than on a cold day. Which explanation is best?
choices: Warm air only dries the dough, so it rises by taking in water
Warmth makes the yeast enzymes work faster, so the yeast respires faster and makes CO₂ gas faster
Warmth makes the yeast produce oxygen, which pushes the dough up
Warmth kills the yeast, and the dead yeast makes the dough swell
quiz.rationale: Warmth increases the activity of the enzymes of respiration in yeast. More CO₂ is produced and the gas makes the dough rise faster.
quiz.placement: Predict: question 3 on the mandazi dough in Gikomba Market

quiz.prompt: Which word equation correctly shows aerobic respiration?
choices: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
Glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy
Glucose + carbon dioxide → oxygen + water + energy
Carbon dioxide + water + energy → glucose + oxygen
quiz.rationale: In aerobic respiration glucose reacts with oxygen to give carbon dioxide, water and energy. The first choice is anaerobic respiration in yeast and the third is photosynthesis.
quiz.placement: Part A: structured reading 'Two Roads to Energy: Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration'

quiz.prompt: In the yeast investigation, Tube B was set up with water that had been boiled and cooled, and a 1 cm layer of cooking oil was poured on top. Why were these two steps done?
choices: To make the yeast grow faster by keeping it warm
To add more glucose to the mixture
To remove or keep out oxygen, so the yeast can only respire anaerobically
To stop CO₂ from being made at all
quiz.rationale: Boiling drives out dissolved oxygen and the oil layer stops air from entering. This makes Tube B anaerobic so it can be compared with Tube A, which has air.
quiz.placement: Part B: Yeast CO₂ Investigation, setting up Tube A (aerobic) and Tube B (anaerobic)

quiz.prompt: A group tests how much CO₂ yeast makes. They score the limewater from 0 (clear) to 3 (milky-white). Tube A scores at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes were 0, 1, 1, 2 and 3. What is the total turbidity score for Tube A?
quiz.rationale: Add the scores at all five time points: 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7.
quiz.placement: Part B: Yeast CO₂ Investigation, calculating the total turbidity score for each tube at the 20-minute mark

quiz.prompt: In a yeast investigation, the limewater connected to the anaerobic tube (no oxygen, oil layer on top) turned milky after 15 minutes. What does this show?
choices: The oil layer produced the CO₂
Yeast needs oxygen to make CO₂
Anaerobic respiration releases oxygen
Yeast can make CO₂ without oxygen, so anaerobic respiration also releases CO₂
quiz.rationale: Limewater turns milky when CO₂ is present. CO₂ was made in the tube with no oxygen, so anaerobic respiration in yeast also produces CO₂.
quiz.placement: Part A: Data Analysis & Equation Construction, question 1 (what Tube B tells you about CO₂ without oxygen)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly compares aerobic and anaerobic respiration in yeast?
choices: Both need oxygen, but only anaerobic respiration makes CO₂
Both release the same amount of energy, but anaerobic respiration makes water
Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and releases more energy; anaerobic respiration needs no oxygen, releases less energy and makes ethanol and CO₂
Aerobic respiration needs no oxygen and gives less energy; anaerobic respiration needs oxygen and gives more energy
quiz.rationale: Aerobic respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy) needs oxygen and releases more energy. Anaerobic respiration in yeast (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy) needs no oxygen and releases less energy.
quiz.placement: Part A: Data Analysis & Equation Construction and Part B: Whole-Class Equation Gallery (aerobic and anaerobic equations)

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki leaves in warm water gave off more bubbles than leaves in cold water. Which statement is the best scientific response, based on what yeast respiration showed?
choices: Enzymes are not affected by temperature, so warmth cannot change the bubbles
Warm water may speed up the enzymes of respiration so cells make CO₂ faster; the bubbles should be tested with limewater to be sure
Warm water makes the leaf stop respiring, so the bubbles must come from photosynthesis
Warm water proves that the bubbles are CO₂ from respiration, so no further test is needed
quiz.rationale: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions, and warmth increases their activity, so respiration and CO₂ production may be faster. We tested yeast, not the leaf bubbles, so this is a hypothesis that needs a limewater test.
quiz.placement: Part C: Connecting to Phenomenon (warm and cold water sukuma wiki bubbles, including the word ENZYME)

quiz.prompt: A student draws a plant cell to show respiration. Where should the student label the site of aerobic respiration, and where does anaerobic respiration (making ethanol and CO₂) start?
choices: Aerobic in the stoma; anaerobic in the guard cell
Both in the cell wall
Aerobic in the mitochondrion; anaerobic in the cytoplasm
Aerobic in the cytoplasm; anaerobic in the mitochondrion
quiz.rationale: The mitochondrion is the site of aerobic respiration and needs oxygen. Anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm without oxygen.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the zoomed-in plant cell layer (mitochondrion, aerobic BLUE and anaerobic RED pathways) to the cumulative model

lessons.title: Importance of Anaerobic Respiration: From Busaa to Biogas

quiz.prompt: Mama Wanjiku mixes yeast, flour, sugar and warm water to make mandazi dough. After some time the dough rises and is full of air pockets. Which gas mainly fills these pockets, and where does it come from?
choices: Oxygen, released by the flour as the dough warms
Carbon dioxide, made by the yeast when it respires without oxygen
Methane, made when the sugar is mixed into the dough
Water vapour, made when the flour dissolves in water
quiz.rationale: Yeast breaks down sugar by anaerobic respiration inside the dough, where oxygen is limited. This releases carbon dioxide, which gets trapped and makes the dough rise.
quiz.placement: Predict: mandazi dough images and prediction questions (a) and (b)

quiz.prompt: Uji made from millet in western Kenya is left to ferment and becomes sour. Which product of anaerobic respiration makes the uji taste sour?
choices: Oxygen, made by the millet grains
Ethanol, made by yeast
Lactic acid, made by bacteria
Methane, made in a biogas digester
quiz.rationale: Bacteria in fermenting uji break down sugars without oxygen and produce lactic acid, which gives the sour taste. Ethanol is the product when yeast ferments, as in busaa.
quiz.placement: Part A: Gallery Walk, Station 1 (Uji Fermentation)

quiz.prompt: Which word equation correctly shows anaerobic respiration in yeast, as in busaa brewing and mandazi dough?
choices: Ethanol + carbon dioxide → glucose + energy
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
Glucose → lactic acid + energy
Glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy
quiz.rationale: In yeast, glucose is broken down without oxygen into ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing a small amount of energy. The equation with oxygen is aerobic respiration, and lactic acid is made by bacteria and animal muscle.
quiz.placement: Part B: Explain the Phenomenon, Sentence 2 (word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast)

quiz.prompt: Three identical bottles each hold 200 mL of warm water (37 °C) and 1 teaspoon of sugar, with a balloon over the mouth. Bottle A has no yeast, Bottle B has 1 g of yeast and Bottle C has 2 g of yeast. After 10 minutes, which bottle's balloon is inflated the most, and why?
choices: All three equally, because they have the same amount of sugar
Bottle B, because a medium amount of yeast works best
Bottle A, because sugar alone makes the most gas
Bottle C, because more yeast ferments the sugar faster and makes more carbon dioxide
quiz.rationale: More yeast means faster fermentation of the sugar, so more carbon dioxide is released to inflate the balloon. Bottle A has no yeast, so almost no gas is made.
quiz.placement: Part B: Live Demo (yeast, sugar and balloon bottles A, B and C)

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki roots in flooded (waterlogged) soil can produce ethanol and carbon dioxide. Why do the roots respire anaerobically in this situation?
choices: Water fills the soil spaces, so very little oxygen reaches the roots
The roots have run out of glucose to use
Waterlogged soil has too much oxygen for the roots to use
Plant roots always respire anaerobically, whatever the soil conditions
quiz.rationale: In waterlogged soil the air spaces are filled with water, so oxygen is limited and the root cells switch to anaerobic respiration. This produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, as in yeast.
quiz.placement: Part A: Gallery Walk, Station 6 (Alcoholic Fermentation in Waterlogged Plant Roots)

quiz.prompt: A student adds an anaerobic branch to their respiration model and labels the energy released from one glucose molecule. Which label is correct when comparing it with aerobic respiration?
choices: Anaerobic: 0 ATP, because no energy is released without oxygen
Anaerobic: 36–38 ATP, the same as aerobic respiration
Anaerobic: 2 ATP, much more than the 36–38 ATP from aerobic respiration
Anaerobic: 2 ATP, much less than the 36–38 ATP from aerobic respiration
quiz.rationale: Anaerobic respiration releases only about 2 ATP per glucose, while aerobic respiration releases 36–38 ATP. This is the trade-off of respiring without oxygen.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the ANAEROBIC BRANCH with the '2 ATP' label to the cumulative respiration model

quiz.prompt: On a dairy farm in Kisumu, cow dung and plant waste are placed in a closed digester. Microbes break the waste down and produce methane gas for cooking. Which statement about this process is correct?
choices: It is aerobic respiration, because the microbes need plenty of oxygen
It is anaerobic respiration, because the microbes break down the waste without oxygen
It is neither, because methane cannot be made by living things
It is photosynthesis, because plant waste is used
quiz.rationale: The sealed digester has little or no oxygen. The microbes break down the dung and plant waste by anaerobic respiration, and the methane they produce is used as fuel.
quiz.placement: Part A: Gallery Walk, Station 4 (Biogas Digester, Kisumu dairy farm)

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Respiration Rate: Temperature, Glucose, and Oxygen

quiz.prompt: A group tests how temperature affects yeast respiration using three bottles at 10 °C, 37 °C and 55 °C. Which change would make this a NOT fair test?
choices: Using bottles of the same size for every temperature
Counting bubbles for 1 minute at each temperature
Using 5 g of yeast in the 10 °C bottle but 10 g of yeast in the 37 °C bottle
Using 100 mL of the same 10% sugar-cane juice solution in every bottle
quiz.rationale: In a fair test only the independent variable (temperature) changes. Different amounts of yeast would be a second variable that also changes the bubble count.
quiz.placement: Station A — Temperature Effect: three beakers at 10, 37 and 55 degrees C

quiz.prompt: In the yeast investigation, students counted CO2 bubbles coming out of a tube each minute. What does the number of bubbles per minute tell us?
choices: How much water the yeast has absorbed
How much heat the sugar solution has lost
How much oxygen the yeast has stored
How fast the yeast is respiring, because CO2 is a product of respiration
quiz.rationale: CO2 is released when yeast breaks down glucose, so bubbles per minute is used as a proxy for the respiration rate.
quiz.placement: Teacher probing question: 'What does each bubble represent in terms of chemistry?'

quiz.prompt: The yeast bottle kept in ice-cold water (10 °C) produced almost no bubbles. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Cold water makes yeast respire without producing CO2
Respiration has stopped completely because cold kills yeast
Respiration is happening very slowly because enzymes work slowly at low temperature
Yeast does not respire in water
quiz.rationale: Few bubbles means a very slow rate, not zero. At low temperature molecules have less kinetic energy, so enzyme-substrate collisions are less frequent.
quiz.placement: Explain: whole-class discussion of the temperature trend (Station A)

quiz.prompt: A group counted 3 bubbles per minute at 10 °C and 24 bubbles per minute at 37 °C. How many times faster was the bubble rate at 37 °C than at 10 °C?
choices: 21 times
27 times
8 times
72 times
quiz.rationale: Divide the higher rate by the lower rate: 24 ÷ 3 = 8, so the rate was 8 times faster.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning sentences for temperature (3 and 24 bubbles per minute)

quiz.prompt: In the temperature investigation, the rate of respiration rises as the temperature goes up to about 37 °C. Why would the rate fall again if the yeast were kept at a much higher temperature, well above its enzymes' optimum?
choices: The enzymes become more active because they have more kinetic energy
The sugar turns into oxygen at high temperature
The enzymes lose their shape (denature) and can no longer break down glucose
Yeast cells become stronger and need less glucose
quiz.rationale: Above the optimum temperature the enzymes denature, so substrate no longer fits the active site and the rate of glucose breakdown falls. It is not that heat makes yeast stronger.
quiz.placement: Explain: Reasoning sentence linking temperature to enzyme activity and denaturation

quiz.prompt: Yeast was placed in 2%, 10% and 20% sugar solutions at room temperature. The rate rises with sugar concentration, but would level off at very high concentrations. What is the best explanation for levelling off?
choices: All the enzyme active sites are already occupied (saturated), so extra glucose cannot be used faster
The extra sugar changes into oxygen
Enzymes are destroyed by sugar at every concentration
The yeast stops being alive as soon as sugar is added
quiz.rationale: More substrate increases the rate until the enzymes are saturated. After that, adding more glucose cannot increase the rate.
quiz.placement: Station B — Sugar Concentration Effect: 2%, 10% and undiluted sugar-cane juice (about 20%)

quiz.prompt: Two yeast bottles at 37 °C contain the same juice. One has air above the juice and the other has a layer of cooking oil that keeps air out. The oil-covered bottle still produces CO2 bubbles. Which statement is correct?
choices: The oil-covered bottle respires anaerobically, so it can release CO2 but makes only about 2 ATP per glucose
More CO2 bubbles always means more ATP is made
Bubbles in the oil-covered bottle must be oxygen coming from the oil
The oil-covered bottle is respiring aerobically and makes 36 to 38 ATP per glucose
quiz.rationale: With oxygen excluded, yeast ferments glucose anaerobically. CO2 is still released but the ATP yield is about 2, compared with 36 to 38 for aerobic respiration, so CO2 amount does not show ATP yield.
quiz.placement: Station C — Oxygen Availability Effect: shaken bottle versus oil-covered bottle

quiz.prompt: A student says: 'Yeast is not a plant, so our yeast results tell us nothing about sukuma wiki leaves.' What is the best reply?
choices: Yeast and kale cannot be compared because only animals respire
Yeast is an animal cell, so its results are the same as kale
Yeast is a plant, so the results apply exactly to kale
Yeast is a single-celled fungus, so it is only a model. Plant, animal and fungal cells all respire, so it suggests what leaf cells do, but leaves still need to be tested
quiz.rationale: Yeast is a fungus and is used as a model. All these cells release energy by respiration, so the yeast results suggest what happens in leaf cells, but the leaf must still be tested.
quiz.placement: Explain: misconception 'Yeast is not a plant, so these results do not apply to sukuma wiki'

lessons.title: Adaptations for Gaseous Exchange in Different Environments

quiz.prompt: Before looking closely at three plants, a student predicts: "The cactus from Turkana has no stomata, because it lives in a very dry place." Which statement best corrects this idea?
choices: Cacti have more stomata than any other plant, all on the upper surface of the leaf
Cacti have stomata, but they are sunken, which helps reduce water loss while still allowing gas exchange
Cacti have no stomata, so they take in gases directly through the cuticle
Cacti have stomata, but they stay permanently open to take in as much air as possible
quiz.rationale: Xerophytes such as cacti and acacia do have stomata, but these are sunken in pits (usually on the stem in cacti). This reduces water loss while gas exchange still happens.
quiz.placement: Station A: xerophyte (cactus or flat-spined acacia) observation

quiz.prompt: An acacia tree in the Rift Valley has stomata sunken in small pits below the leaf surface. Why does this help the tree survive in hot, dry conditions?
choices: The pit blocks all gas movement so that no water can escape
The pit lets more sunlight reach the stoma so that it opens wider
The pit traps moist air around the stoma, which slows the evaporation of water vapour from the leaf
The pit lets the leaf absorb water directly from the dry air
quiz.rationale: Moist air trapped in the pit reduces the water vapour gradient above the stoma, so less water evaporates while gases can still diffuse.
quiz.placement: Whole-class CER discussion: claim that sunken stomata in acacia reduce water loss without preventing gas exchange

quiz.prompt: Water hyacinth floats on Lake Victoria near Kisumu. Where would you expect to find most of its stomata, and why?
choices: On both surfaces equally, because the plant needs water from both sides
On the lower surface, because the lower surface touches the water
On the upper surface, because the upper surface faces the air
Only on the roots, because the roots are under water
quiz.rationale: The upper (adaxial) surface of a floating leaf faces the air, so stomata are found there. Stomata on the lower surface would be blocked by water.
quiz.placement: Station B: hydrophyte (water hyacinth) observation

quiz.prompt: The submerged roots and stems of a water hyacinth in a waterlogged habitat contain large air spaces called aerenchyma. What is their main job in gaseous exchange?
choices: They stop carbon dioxide from leaving the plant
They make the cuticle thicker to keep water out
They store water for the plant to use during droughts
They give internal channels so that oxygen can diffuse to submerged tissues
quiz.rationale: Aerenchyma are air-filled channels. Oxygen from the air diffuses along them to tissues under water, where little oxygen is available.
quiz.placement: Whole-class discussion: aerenchyma in the water hyacinth at the Lake Victoria station

quiz.prompt: A student says: "Aerenchyma is a feature of xerophytes because they need to store air in the desert." Which plant type is aerenchyma actually an adaptation of?
choices: All plants have it equally
Hydrophytes, such as water hyacinth
Mesophytes, such as sukuma wiki
Xerophytes, such as the cactus
quiz.rationale: Aerenchyma is an adaptation of hydrophytes living in waterlogged conditions. Labelling it as a xerophyte feature is a common model error.
quiz.placement: Model revision: three annotated panels (Turkana xerophyte / Lake Victoria hydrophyte / Nairobi mesophyte)

quiz.prompt: Compare the cuticle of a cactus from Turkana with the cuticle of sukuma wiki grown in a Nairobi school garden. Which statement is correct?
choices: The cactus has a thin cuticle, because it needs to absorb water through its surface
The cactus has a thick cuticle, which reduces water loss in a hot, dry environment
Sukuma wiki has a thicker cuticle, because Nairobi has more rainfall
Both have equally thin cuticles because both have stomata
quiz.rationale: Xerophytes have a thick cuticle that cuts water loss through the surface. Mesophytes like sukuma wiki have a moderate cuticle suited to moderate conditions.
quiz.placement: Station C: mesophyte (sukuma wiki) cuticle compared with the cactus station

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki is a mesophyte growing where rainfall and temperature are moderate. Which description of its leaf best fits this environment?
choices: No stomata and gas exchange through lenticels only
Stomata mainly on the lower surface, a moderate cuticle and a broad leaf
Stomata buried deep in pits and a very thick cuticle
Large air spaces throughout the leaf and stomata only on the upper surface
quiz.rationale: Mesophytes show a typical arrangement: stomata mostly on the lower surface, a moderate cuticle and a broad leaf. They have no extreme adaptations for dryness or waterlogging.
quiz.placement: Station C: mesophyte (sukuma wiki) observation

quiz.prompt: Which pairing of plant, environment and adaptation for gaseous exchange is correct?
choices: Acacia, Rift Valley, sunken stomata and reduced leaf area
Sukuma wiki, Nairobi garden, aerenchyma throughout the stem
Water hyacinth, Lake Victoria, thick cuticle and sunken stomata
Cactus, Turkana, floating leaves with stomata on the upper surface
quiz.rationale: Acacia is a xerophyte of dry areas such as the Rift Valley, and shows sunken stomata and reduced leaf area to cut water loss. The other pairings give hydrophyte or mesophyte features to the wrong plant.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: three-way comparison of xerophytes, hydrophytes and mesophytes

lessons.title: Photosynthesis, Gaseous Exchange & Respiration Linkages: Systems Synthesis and Model Building

quiz.prompt: A learner draws arrows to show how photosynthesis and cellular respiration depend on each other in a sukuma wiki plant. Which arrow is correct?
choices: CO₂ released by respiration is used as a raw material for photosynthesis
Photosynthesis uses up O₂ and releases CO₂ for respiration
Glucose moves out of the leaf through the stomata to be used in respiration
Respiration produces O₂ which photosynthesis then uses to make ATP
quiz.rationale: Respiration releases CO₂, which can be used in photosynthesis. Glucose is not released through stomata. Photosynthesis releases O₂ and respiration uses it, not the other way round.
quiz.placement: Individual Prediction Mapping: drawing labelled arrows between the three boxes

quiz.prompt: During evidence card sorting, a group places the card 'C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP' in the OVERLAP zone. Which reason best explains why this card connects the processes?
choices: ATP is the gas that moves in and out of the stomata
Glucose is made in respiration and then used up by photosynthesis
The CO₂ and O₂ shown here are exchanged with photosynthesis, which releases the O₂ and uses the CO₂
Respiration only happens when photosynthesis is also happening
quiz.rationale: Respiration uses O₂ (made by photosynthesis) and releases CO₂ (used by photosynthesis), so the same molecules link the two processes. Glucose is a product of photosynthesis and a reactant in respiration. ATP is not a gas.
quiz.placement: Evidence Card Sorting: placing cards in the OVERLAP zone and justifying with molecular flow

quiz.prompt: At night, a sukuma wiki plant in the school garden has its stomata closed and there is no light. Which statement about this plant is correct?
choices: Respiration stops because the plant does not need energy at night
Photosynthesis continues using the O₂ made by respiration
Photosynthesis stops but respiration continues, and less CO₂ enters because the stomata are closed
Both photosynthesis and respiration continue, but at a slower rate
quiz.rationale: Photosynthesis needs light, so it stops at night. Respiration happens all the time in living cells, and closed stomata reduce the entry of CO₂.
quiz.placement: Colour-Coded Systems Diagram: annotation of what happens at night versus during the day

quiz.prompt: In a sukuma wiki leaf cell, where do photosynthesis and aerobic respiration take place?
choices: Both processes in the stomata
Both processes in the chloroplast
Photosynthesis in the chloroplast and respiration in the mitochondrion
Photosynthesis in the mitochondrion and respiration in the chloroplast
quiz.rationale: The chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis and the mitochondrion is the site of aerobic respiration. Stomata are pores for gas movement and are not sites of either process.
quiz.placement: Colour-Coded Systems Diagram: chloroplast and mitochondrion drawn inside a cell

quiz.prompt: A learner writes a green sticky note answering the question 'Why is gaseous exchange important to plants?' Which note gives the best answer?
choices: Plants must breathe in and out with lungs like animals do
Gaseous exchange is only needed in the day because plants respire only in the light
CO₂ must get in for photosynthesis and O₂ must get in for respiration, through stomata, lenticels and the cuticle
Gaseous exchange lets glucose escape from the leaf so it does not build up
quiz.rationale: Plants need CO₂ for photosynthesis and O₂ for respiration, and gas enters through structures such as stomata and lenticels. Plants do not have lungs, glucose is not lost through stomata, and respiration goes on day and night.
quiz.placement: Dual Sticky-Note DQB Protocol: green 'Now I can answer…' notes

quiz.prompt: Mwalimu Njoroge's class saw more bubbles from sukuma wiki leaves in warm water than in cold water. The gas in the bubbles was never tested. Which statement is the most scientifically honest conclusion?
choices: The bubbles are definitely oxygen from photosynthesis, so warm water must make photosynthesis stop
Warm water has no effect, because bubbles come only from the stomata
Warmth may speed up enzyme-controlled reactions and make gas in the leaf expand and dissolve less, but the gas in the bubbles was not tested
The bubbles are CO₂ because plants only respire and do not photosynthesise
quiz.rationale: Higher temperature can raise reaction rates and make gas expand and dissolve less, giving more bubbles. The identity of the gas was not tested, so it cannot be claimed as certain.
quiz.placement: Model Narrative: Sentence 3 explaining why warm water produced more bubbles and what was not tested

quiz.prompt: A mango tree has woody stems with no stomata. Which structure allows the living cells in the stem to take in O₂ for respiration and release CO₂?
choices: Chloroplasts
Root hairs only
Guard cells on the leaf surface
Lenticels
quiz.rationale: Lenticels are small openings in woody stems that let O₂ in and CO₂ out for respiration. Guard cells control stomata on leaves, and chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: linking gaseous exchange structures (stomata, lenticels, cuticle) to the whole system

lessons.title: Project Launch & Planning: Investigating Anaerobic Respiration with Local Kenyan Materials

quiz.prompt: A mandazi vendor in Nairobi leaves her dough in a covered bowl. After some time the dough rises and is full of tiny gas bubbles. What is the best explanation for the gas in the dough?
choices: The flour itself slowly releases oxygen gas into the dough.
Yeast cells in the dough break down sugar without much oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
The dough is breathing in oxygen from the air in exactly the same way a kale leaf does.
Warm air from the kitchen is pushed into the dough as it rests.
quiz.rationale: Yeast in the dough respires anaerobically (fermentation), breaking down sugar and releasing CO₂, which makes the dough rise. The dough does not simply breathe like a leaf, and flour does not release oxygen.
quiz.placement: Think-Pair-Share on the two images: sukuma wiki bubbles and the mandazi dough rising

quiz.prompt: A bottle contains sugar solution and baker's yeast, with a balloon stretched over the neck. After some time the balloon inflates. Which gas has mainly inflated the balloon, and which process made it?
choices: Hydrogen, made when sugar dissolves in water
Oxygen, made by photosynthesis in the yeast
Water vapour, made by aerobic respiration in the sugar
Carbon dioxide, made by anaerobic respiration (fermentation) in the yeast
quiz.rationale: Yeast ferments sugar without oxygen to make ethanol and carbon dioxide. The CO₂ gas is what inflates the balloon.
quiz.placement: Gallery Walk, Station A: Yeast Fermentation (balloon over the bottle neck)

quiz.prompt: At Station B, vegetable scraps such as sukuma wiki offcuts and ugali remnants are placed in a sealed plastic bottle, and gas is collected from it. Why does the bottle need to be sealed for the biogas simulation?
choices: Sealing stops the vegetable scraps from ever producing gas on their own.
Sealing makes the microbes use more oxygen, so more gas is produced.
Sealing is only needed to keep flies away; it does not change the process.
Sealing keeps oxygen out, so microbes break down the waste by anaerobic respiration and release gas.
quiz.rationale: Biogas is produced by microbes respiring anaerobically. A sealed bottle keeps oxygen out, which is the condition needed for this process, as in farm biogas digesters.
quiz.placement: Gallery Walk, Station B: Biogas Simulation (sealed bottle of kitchen scraps with tube to inverted water-filled bottle)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes anaerobic respiration in yeast?
choices: Glucose is broken down to lactic acid and carbon dioxide, with a lot of energy released.
Glucose is broken down to carbon dioxide and water, with a lot of energy released.
Glucose is broken down using oxygen to make ethanol and water.
Glucose is broken down without oxygen to ethanol and carbon dioxide, with a little energy released.
quiz.rationale: In yeast, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) gives ethanol and CO₂ plus a small amount of ATP. Lactic acid is made in muscle cells and some bacteria, and CO₂ + water + lots of ATP describes aerobic respiration.
quiz.placement: Whole-class explanation using the 'Two Pathways' diagram

quiz.prompt: A student writes this Connection Sentence: 'Anaerobic respiration is similar to aerobic respiration in plants because both ______, but different because ______.' Which pair of phrases completes it correctly?
choices: both happen only in plant leaves / anaerobic respiration happens only in animals
both always produce carbon dioxide and ethanol / anaerobic respiration makes water
both start with glucose and release energy / anaerobic respiration does not use oxygen and releases less energy
both need oxygen to work / anaerobic respiration makes more ATP
quiz.rationale: Both pathways break down glucose to release energy. Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and releases less ATP, with different end-products such as ethanol or lactic acid.
quiz.placement: Connection Sentence: 'Anaerobic respiration is similar to what we observed in sukuma wiki leaves because ___, but it is different because ___'

quiz.prompt: A group plans to test how the temperature of the sugar solution affects fermentation. They set up three bottles, each with sugar, yeast and water, at 20 °C, 30 °C and 40 °C. Each bottle has a balloon on top, and they measure the balloon diameter after 20 minutes. What is the dependent variable?
choices: The type of bottle used
The temperature of the sugar solution
The balloon diameter after 20 minutes
The mass of yeast added to each bottle
quiz.rationale: The dependent variable is what is measured as the result of the change. Here the balloon diameter shows how much CO₂ was produced. Temperature is the independent variable, the thing changed.
quiz.placement: Project Planning Template: independent and dependent variables

quiz.prompt: In the same investigation (sugar, yeast and water in bottles at 20 °C, 30 °C and 40 °C, each with a balloon), which of these must be kept the same in all three bottles as a controlled variable?
choices: The temperature of the solution
The amount of carbon dioxide produced
The mass of yeast and the volume of water
The balloon diameter after 20 minutes
quiz.rationale: Controlled variables are kept constant so that only temperature changes. Mass of yeast and volume of water must be equal. Temperature is the variable being changed, and balloon size and CO₂ are the results being measured.
quiz.placement: Project Planning Template: at least 3 controlled variables

quiz.prompt: Kale leaf cells normally respire using oxygen. Suppose a leaf's cells were kept without any oxygen. Based on this lesson, what would you expect?
choices: The cells could only release a little energy from glucose, and their end-products would be different.
The cells would stop needing glucose because respiration is no longer needed.
The cells would respire faster and release more energy than before.
The cells would make oxygen from the glucose to continue aerobic respiration.
quiz.rationale: Without oxygen, glucose can only be broken down by anaerobic respiration. This releases much less energy and gives different end-products, such as ethanol and CO₂ in yeast.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: connecting the anaerobic investigation back to the sukuma wiki bubbles from Lesson 1

lessons.title: Project Execution: Carrying Out Investigations on Plant Gaseous Exchange and Respiration

quiz.prompt: A group is testing how water temperature (10°C, 25°C and 40°C) affects gas production by yeast in sugar solution. They count the bubbles from the delivery tube every minute. Which one is the dependent variable?
choices: Mass of yeast used
Amount of sugar used
Water temperature (10°C, 25°C, 40°C)
Number of bubbles per minute
quiz.rationale: The dependent variable is what is measured as the result, here bubbles per minute. Temperature is the independent variable, while sugar and yeast mass are controlled variables.
quiz.placement: Groups identify their independent variable, dependent variable and at least two controlled variables on a sticky note

quiz.prompt: In a yeast investigation, a group adds a 1 cm layer of cooking oil on top of the yeast and sugar mixture. What is the purpose of the oil layer?
choices: To make the bubbles larger
To keep the mixture warm
To exclude air so that any gas produced is made without oxygen
To give the yeast extra food
quiz.rationale: The oil floats on the surface and stops air from reaching the yeast. Any gas produced is therefore made without oxygen, which tests for anaerobic respiration (fermentation).
quiz.placement: Part A: Yeast fermentation investigation with a 1 cm cooking-oil layer to exclude air

quiz.prompt: During a yeast investigation, one bubble count is very different from the other readings in the table. What should the group do?
choices: Record it honestly and ask what might have caused it
Stop the investigation and start again
Change it so that it matches the other readings
Cross it out at once because it must be a mistake
quiz.rationale: Honest scientists record all readings, including unexpected ones. An unusual reading may be real evidence, so the group should look for a possible cause before deciding anything.
quiz.placement: Teacher anomaly probe during circulation: 'Before you cross it out, ask yourselves, could that be real?'

quiz.prompt: A group puts yeast in sugar solution at 40°C. In Trial 1 they count 22 bubbles per minute. In Trial 2 they count 26 bubbles per minute. What is the mean number of bubbles per minute?
quiz.rationale: Mean = (22 + 26) ÷ 2 = 48 ÷ 2 = 24 bubbles per minute.
quiz.placement: Part A: groups conduct at least two trials and begin calculating means at the 30-minute mark

quiz.prompt: A group found that yeast in sugar solution at 40°C made more gas than at 25°C. Which sentence is the best reasoning to explain this result?
choices: Warm water makes the yeast breathe in more oxygen from the air.
Warmth increases the activity of enzymes in yeast cells, so fermentation of sugar is faster and more carbon dioxide is released.
Yeast needs stomata to open wider in warm water.
The temperature made more bubbles because higher temperature increased the number of bubbles.
quiz.rationale: Good reasoning links the data to a biological process: enzymes in yeast work faster in warmth, so fermentation releases CO₂ faster. The first option only repeats the claim and is circular.
quiz.placement: Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) written explanation for each group's findings

quiz.prompt: One group found that yeast in sugar solution under a layer of oil still produced gas. Another group found that a warmer sugar solution produced more gas. Together, what do these two findings suggest?
choices: Yeast needs oxygen to make gas, and cold speeds up the process
Yeast can make carbon dioxide without oxygen, and warmth speeds up the process
The oil itself produces the gas, and warmth has no effect
Yeast only makes gas in cold water without sugar
quiz.rationale: Gas under the oil layer shows CO₂ is made without oxygen (fermentation). More gas in warmth shows that temperature increases the rate of the process.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: teacher narrates connections between Group 3's oil-layer claim and Group 1's temperature claim

quiz.prompt: Fermentation (anaerobic respiration) releases energy from glucose and produces carbon dioxide. Where in a plant or yeast cell does fermentation take place?
choices: In the cytoplasm of the cell
In the guard cells only
In the cuticle covering the leaf
In the stomata on the leaf surface
quiz.rationale: Fermentation happens inside the cell, in the cytoplasm. Stomata, guard cells and the cuticle are structures involved in gas exchange at the leaf surface, not the site of fermentation.
quiz.placement: Model revision: teacher prompt 'Where would you add the cytoplasm and the fermentation equation to your model?'

quiz.prompt: In a biogas simulation, a group puts chopped kitchen scraps in water in a bottle with a delivery tube to an inverted water-filled bottle. Gas collects very slowly. Why do they compare their bottle with one the teacher started 2 to 3 days earlier?
choices: Because the older bottle will have no gas, which gives a fair control
Because the teacher's bottle uses a different gas
Because older bottles always give less gas than new ones
Because gas from waste builds up slowly, so the older bottle shows what the gas production looks like after several days
quiz.rationale: Microorganisms break down waste slowly, so gas collects over days. The earlier-started bottle lets the group see the later stage of the process within one lesson.
quiz.placement: Part B: Biogas simulation, comparing with a teacher-prepared bottle started 2 to 3 days earlier

lessons.title: Project Presentations and Peer Review: Communicating Evidence on Plant Gaseous Exchange and Respiration

quiz.prompt: A group claims: "Warmer temperature increased the rate of respiration in yeast." Which piece of evidence best supports this claim?
choices: Yeast is a fungus that is used to make mandazi and uji.
Our group worked well together during the experiment.
Yeast at 35 °C made 24 bubbles per minute, but yeast at 15 °C made only 6 bubbles per minute.
The yeast mixture smelled stronger than the other groups' mixtures.
quiz.rationale: Good evidence for a CER claim is measured data that compares the conditions. The two bubble rates at different temperatures directly show how temperature changed the rate. The other choices are background facts or opinions, not data.
quiz.placement: Predict: half-sheet prompt asking each group to write its strongest CER claim

quiz.prompt: One group's results show that at 25 °C the yeast made fewer bubbles than at 15 °C, which they did not expect. What should the group do when presenting?
choices: Report the result honestly and suggest reasons for it, such as a leaking tube or different amounts of yeast.
Leave out that result so the claim looks stronger.
Say that the experiment failed and that the whole investigation is useless.
Change the number so that it fits the expected pattern.
quiz.rationale: Scientists report anomalous data honestly and try to explain it by thinking about variables that may have affected the result. Hiding or changing data is dishonest, and an unexpected result is still useful evidence.
quiz.placement: Poster carousel: groups present their investigations and report anomalous results honestly

quiz.prompt: In a yeast fermentation experiment, a group sealed the tube so that no air could enter. After 8 minutes the limewater connected to the tube turned cloudy. What does this show?
choices: Water vapour was the only gas released.
Oxygen was produced by the yeast.
The yeast produced carbon dioxide even without oxygen (anaerobic respiration).
The yeast made its own food by photosynthesis.
quiz.rationale: Limewater turns cloudy when carbon dioxide is present. Because the tube was sealed from air, the CO2 came from anaerobic respiration (fermentation).
quiz.placement: Poster carousel: yeast fermentation group presents its sealed-tube limewater result

quiz.prompt: Three groups used different investigations (yeast fermentation, biogas simulation and uji fermentation). All three found that CO2 was produced when oxygen was limited. Why does this increase confidence in the conclusion?
choices: Because the teacher agrees with the conclusion.
Because several independent investigations reaching the same finding builds scientific consensus.
Because the groups all used the same apparatus and the same materials.
Because three groups is a bigger number than one, whatever the evidence.
quiz.rationale: When multiple independent investigations converge on the same finding, confidence in the conclusion increases. This is called scientific consensus.
quiz.placement: Whole-class argumentation discussion: the teacher introduces the term 'scientific consensus'

quiz.prompt: A student says: "Plants do not really breathe. They only make food by photosynthesis." Which reply is best supported by scientific evidence?
choices: Plants respire only at night, so they do nothing with gases during the day.
Plants do not need oxygen because they make their own food.
Photosynthesis and respiration are the same process, so plants do both together.
All living plant cells respire to release energy. This releases CO2, and it leaves the plant through stomata and lenticels.
quiz.rationale: Respiration happens in all living cells all the time, including plant cells, and it releases CO2. Photosynthesis is a different process. Plants exchange gases with the air through stomata and lenticels.
quiz.placement: Whole-class argumentation discussion, question 3: arguing back that plants do not really breathe

quiz.prompt: Yeast was placed in warm water (35 °C) and in cold water (10 °C). The warm mixture produced many more CO2 bubbles. Which explanation is best?
choices: Warm water makes the yeast produce gas through photosynthesis.
Warm water contains more oxygen than cold water, so the yeast makes food.
The enzymes that control respiration work faster at a warmer temperature, so more CO2 is released.
Cold water destroys all the enzymes in the yeast permanently.
quiz.rationale: Respiration is controlled by enzymes. Within a moderate range, higher temperature makes them work faster, so respiration rate and CO2 release increase.
quiz.placement: DQB update: thumbs vote on the Lesson 1 question about why warm water increased bubble production

quiz.prompt: On a hot, dry day at midday, the stomata of a leaf close. Mesophyll cells inside the leaf are still respiring. What happens to the CO2 they produce?
choices: It leaves quickly through the waxy cuticle.
It turns into oxygen straight away, so none builds up.
It is not produced, because respiration stops when stomata close.
It cannot easily leave the leaf, so it builds up inside.
quiz.rationale: Stomata are the main exit for CO2 in a leaf. The waxy cuticle blocks gas movement, and cells keep respiring, so CO2 accumulates inside the leaf until the stomata open again.
quiz.placement: Model revision: extension prompt about closed stomata at midday during drought

lessons.title: Consolidation, Model Finalisation & Unit Review: How Do Plants "Breathe" and Release Energy?

quiz.prompt: In a kale leaf, how do guard cells open a stoma?
choices: The guard cells lose water and shrink, which pulls the stoma open
Air pressure inside the leaf blows the guard cells apart
Potassium ions move into the guard cells, water enters by osmosis, and the guard cells become turgid and bend apart
The guard cells divide to make a gap between them
quiz.rationale: Ions (K⁺) enter the guard cells, water follows by osmosis, and the swollen (turgid) guard cells curve apart to open the stoma. Losing water makes them flaccid and the stoma closes.
quiz.placement: Model Finalisation Checklist, item 2: mechanism of stomatal opening/closing

quiz.prompt: Mangrove trees at Gazi Bay in Kwale County grow in waterlogged mud that has very little oxygen. Why do they have pneumatophores (breathing roots) that stick up into the air?
choices: To make food by photosynthesis in the mud
To absorb more salt from the sea water
To release oxygen so the mud becomes dry
To take in air so the underground roots can get oxygen for aerobic respiration
quiz.rationale: Roots in waterlogged mud cannot get enough oxygen from the soil. Pneumatophores have pores that let air in, so root cells can still respire aerobically and release energy.
quiz.placement: Model Finalisation Checklist, item 4: pneumatophore in a waterlogged environment (Gazi Bay)

quiz.prompt: A tree has a thick, woody stem covered with bark. Which structure lets gases pass between the air and the living cells under the bark?
choices: Lenticels, which are small pores in the bark
Guard cells in the waxy cuticle of the bark
Pneumatophores, which are found on every woody stem
The cuticle, which allows oxygen to pass freely
quiz.rationale: Lenticels are small openings in the bark of woody stems that allow gas exchange. The cuticle is waxy and reduces water loss, and pneumatophores are found only on plants in waterlogged soils.
quiz.placement: Model Finalisation Checklist, item 3: lenticel on a woody stem with gas exchange arrows

quiz.prompt: A plant cell breaks down the same amount of glucose by aerobic respiration and by anaerobic respiration. Which statement is correct?
choices: Aerobic respiration releases much more ATP, because glucose is broken down completely using oxygen
Anaerobic respiration releases much more ATP because it uses no oxygen
Aerobic respiration releases no ATP and only makes heat
Both release the same amount of ATP, but anaerobic respiration is faster
quiz.rationale: In aerobic respiration glucose is broken down completely (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation) and releases far more ATP. Anaerobic respiration only partly breaks it down and releases little ATP.
quiz.placement: Model Finalisation Checklist, items 5 and 6: aerobic respiration pathway and anaerobic respiration pathway with ATP yield

quiz.prompt: A kale leaf is in the dark at night. Its cells respire but cannot photosynthesise. Which gas movement through the stomata is expected?
choices: Only water vapour moves, because gases cannot pass through stomata in the dark
Carbon dioxide leaves the leaf and oxygen enters
Oxygen leaves the leaf and carbon dioxide enters
Oxygen and carbon dioxide both stop moving completely
quiz.rationale: In the dark there is no photosynthesis, so only respiration happens. Respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, so oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves. In bright light photosynthesis can make more oxygen than respiration uses, so net oxygen leaves.
quiz.placement: Model Finalisation Checklist, item 7: relationship between photosynthesis and respiration (net gas exchange)

quiz.prompt: Cut kale leaves in warm water make more bubbles than leaves in cold water. Which explanation is best supported by what the class learned?
choices: Warm water makes the guard cells decide to make new holes in the leaf
Warm water stops respiration so gas is pushed out of the leaf
Warm water speeds up enzymes in respiration, and also makes gas in the leaf expand and dissolve less in the water
Warm water adds extra oxygen into the leaf
quiz.rationale: Respiration is controlled by enzymes, which work faster when warmer (as the yeast data showed). Warmth also makes gas in the leaf expand and dissolve less in water, so more bubbles are seen.
quiz.placement: Final Explanation writing: component 4, why warm water could increase bubble production

quiz.prompt: Mwalimu Njoroge's class saw bubbles coming from kale leaves in warm water. The class never tested what the bubbles contained. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The bubbles are gas from the leaf's air spaces, probably including carbon dioxide from respiration and, in light, oxygen from photosynthesis, but this was not tested
The bubbles are pure oxygen, because plants only make oxygen
The bubbles are pure carbon dioxide, because the leaf is respiring
The bubbles are nitrogen, because this is the main gas in air
quiz.rationale: The bubbles were not analysed, so we can only say what they probably contain. Leaf air spaces hold a mixture of gases that includes respiratory CO₂ and, in light, photosynthetic O₂.
quiz.placement: Final Explanation writing: component 3, what the bubbles probably contain and what was not tested

quiz.prompt: In the class explanation, guard cells were compared to hinges that open and close the stomata like doors. Where does this picture break down?
choices: Guard cells make the bubbles directly by respiring
Guard cells are made of dead cells, so they cannot open
Guard cells open the stomata only when the leaf is under water
Guard cells do not decide anything; they respond to things such as light, water supply and carbon dioxide level
quiz.rationale: Guard cells are living cells that change shape in response to light, water availability and CO₂. They do not make choices, so the idea that they 'decide' is only a simplification.
quiz.placement: Teacher synthesis after the two group readings: stomata as doors, guard cells as hinges, and where the picture breaks
